title: Love and Desire
lead: The Bible speaks of desire in three ways: as a gift of the creation that husband and wife enjoy (Genesis 2:24–25; Proverbs 5:18–19; Song of Songs), as a force that can be turned to harm (Proverbs 7; 2 Samuel 11; 2 Samuel 13), and as a mark of the fall (Genesis 3:16). The Song of Songs is the one book given entirely to the first, and its word for the man's desire, teshuqah (7:10), is the same word as in Genesis 3:16 and Genesis 4:7.

sections.b: After the creation of the woman, the man says 'this at last is bone of my bones' and the narrator adds that they were naked and not ashamed (Genesis 2:23–25). Proverbs 5:18–19 asks a husband to rejoice in the wife of his youth. Ecclesiastes 9:9 says to enjoy life with the wife you love. Paul tells husband and wife not to deprive each other (1 Corinthians 7:3–5). Hebrews 13:4 says the marriage bed is to be kept undefiled. Christian traditions differ on how far desire is good in itself, how it is ordered to children, and how it compares with celibacy, as the cards on the Song of Songs set out.

Genesis 3:16 tells the woman that her desire will be for her husband and that he will rule over her. Genesis 4:7 says that sin desires Cain and he must rule it. The Hebrew word is teshuqah. Interpreters read it as a punishment, as a prediction of how the relation of man and woman will go wrong, or as a desire to master. The Song of Songs uses the word once, of the man's desire for the woman (7:10), without any mention of rule. Phyllis Trible argued that this reverses the curse; others find the echo too thin to carry that weight.
